extraction.name: Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges
extraction.description: A review of visual question answering datasets, evaluation metrics, and algorithms, emphasizing dataset biases and limitations. The paper discusses DAQUAR, COCO-QA, The VQA Dataset (COCO-VQA and SYNTH-VQA), FM-IQA, Visual Genome, Visual7W, and SHAPES, rather than introducing a single primary dataset. It also describes small datasets constructed for experiments on language bias.
extraction.creator: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan (paper authors).
extraction.datePublished: 2017-06-15 (date shown for arXiv version 4 of the review paper).
extraction.inLanguage: FM-IQA was originally collected in Chinese, with English translations made available.
extraction.citeAs: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan. Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges. arXiv:1610.01465v4, 15 June 2017.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: DAQUAR uses images from NYU-DepthV2 and manual and automatic annotations. COCO-QA automatically derives question-answer pairs from COCO image captions using an NLP algorithm. COCO-VQA uses Amazon Mechanical Turk workers to generate three questions per image, followed by answers from a separate pool of workers. SYNTH-VQA uses constructed cartoon scenes. FM-IQA contains human-generated questions and answers. Visual Genome collects free-form questions and questions prompted by specific image regions using descriptive bounding-box annotations. Visual7W sources telling questions from Visual Genome and collects plausible alternative answers from annotators who do not see the image. SHAPES asks each of 244 unique questions about each of 64 images. The review authors also constructed balanced person-presence questions and paraphrased sports questions using the COCO validation split.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Experiments
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: DAQUAR: NYU-DepthV2 images. COCO-QA: COCO images and image captions. COCO-VQA and FM-IQA: COCO images. SYNTH-VQA: synthetic scenes constructed from over 100 objects, 30 animal models, and 20 human cartoon models. Visual Genome: images occurring in both YFCC100M and COCO. Visual7W: 47,300 Visual Genome images also present in COCO. SHAPES: images of shapes with varying arrangements, types, and colors. The review authors' experimental datasets use images and annotations from the COCO validation split.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: FM-IQA was translated from Chinese into English. SYNTH-VQA scenes are assembled from cartoon object, animal, and human models. The Yin and Yang dataset pairs mostly identical synthetic images with a minor change that reverses the correct binary answer. For their person-presence experiment, the review authors used COCO annotations to construct equal numbers of yes and no questions, with three question phrasings and 115,542 questions total. Their sports experiment used three phrasings for each image, producing 15,711 questions about seven common sports.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For COCO-QA question-answer generation, longer caption sentences are broken into smaller chunks for processing by the NLP algorithm.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: COCO-VQA question writers were instructed to 'Stump a smart robot'; a separate pool supplied ten independent answers per question. SYNTH-VQA has three questions per scene and ten ground-truth answers per question. DAQUAR-consensus adds independently collected human ground-truth answers. Visual Genome uses free-form and region-specific question prompting and restricts questions to What, Where, How, When, Who, and Why. Visual7W adds Which questions whose answers are bounding boxes; plausible text alternatives are collected without showing annotators the image. The VQA Dataset's multiple-choice format includes the most frequent human answer, three plausible answers collected without seeing the image, ten popular dataset answers, and randomly selected correct answers to other questions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The VQA Dataset uses ten independently collected answers per question for consensus evaluation; its reported accuracy is min(n/3, 1), where n is the number of annotators agreeing with the predicted answer. Its multiple-choice correct answer is the most frequent annotator response. COCO-VQA inter-human agreement is approximately 83.3%; over 59% of Why questions have fewer than three identical answers. More than 13% of yes/no questions have both yes and no repeated by more than three annotators. DAQUAR-consensus proposes average consensus, which favors popular answers, and min consensus, which requires agreement with at least one annotator.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: COCO-VQA and SYNTH-VQA: ten independent human answers per question and three questions per image or scene. DAQUAR-consensus: an average of five human ground-truth answers per question.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: COCO-QA uses an NLP algorithm to generate question-answer pairs from image captions; the algorithm's name is not specified. DAQUAR annotations are described as manual and automatic, without naming an automatic annotation tool.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: SYNTH-VQA human cartoon models vary in age, gender, and race to provide variation in appearance. These are synthetic model attributes; collection of corresponding personal attributes from real individuals is not described.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Potential VQA applications include assisting blind and visually impaired individuals in obtaining information about web and real-world images, improving human-computer interaction, and retrieving images without metadata or tags. The paper states that language bias limits deployment and that systems restricted to binary answers have limited real-world utility.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: COCO-VQA contains strong language and answer-frequency biases: question-only models achieve approximately 49.6% accuracy; yes/no questions account for about 38% of questions, and almost 59% have yes answers. Question phrasing supplies clues that systems can exploit without adequate image analysis. COCO-QA is dominated by object questions (69.84%). Free-form Visual Genome annotation can produce repeated questions about holistic image content; region-specific prompting was introduced to combat this. Natural imagery has contextual biases, such as street scenes being more likely to contain dogs than zebras. The paper describes SHAPES as completely balanced and free of bias.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: DAQUAR is small, restricted to indoor scenes, and affected by clutter and difficult lighting. COCO-QA contains awkward, grammatically incorrect, and unintelligible automatically generated questions and only four question types. COCO-VQA includes subjective questions, unreliable annotations, and substantial disagreement. FM-IQA's sentence answers make automatic evaluation difficult, while human judging is expensive and slow. Visual Genome and Visual7W have diverse multi-word answers that complicate open-ended evaluation. SHAPES cannot substitute for real-world imagery. The reviewers could not retrieve FM-IQA's English version from its download link, and COCO-VQA test answers were not publicly available. Existing benchmarks are insufficient to establish that an algorithm has solved general VQA; aggregate accuracy can conceal poor performance on rare question types, and multiple-choice systems can exploit answer-choice biases.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training and evaluating visual question answering systems. COCO-VQA provides training, validation, and testing partitions; DAQUAR and COCO-QA provide training and testing question-answer pairs. SHAPES assesses reasoning about shape attributes, positions, and relationships. The review authors' person-presence and sports datasets test language bias and sensitivity to question phrasing. Recommended benchmarking practices include controlling biases, reporting mean performance across question types, and choosing challenging multiple-choice alternatives that cannot be resolved from answer choices alone. VQA systems should also operate without supplied answer choices.
